title: Generate equivalent fractions by multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same number

lesson.title: Same Fraction, More Pieces

steps.say: You already know that one half of a granola bar is the same amount as two quarters, because you have seen it with fraction bars. Today you will learn a quick way to make those matching fractions with numbers, without drawing every time.

visual.caption: One half and two quarters cover the same amount

steps.say: Here is the whole trick. When you cut every piece into the same number of smaller pieces, you get more pieces, but each one is smaller, so the amount stays the same. In numbers, you multiply the top number and the bottom number by the same number. One times two is two, and two times two is four. So one half equals two quarters.

visual.caption: Each half cut into 2 makes quarters

steps.say: Let us try one together. Imagine a chocolate bar from the corner store cut into three equal pieces, and you have two of them. That is two thirds. Now cut every piece into three smaller pieces. Two times three is six on the top, and three times three is nine on the bottom. Two thirds equals six ninths. Look at the bars, the shaded part is exactly the same length.

visual.caption: Two thirds and six ninths are the same amount

steps.say: Now here are two mistakes to watch out for. Some kids add one to the top and one to the bottom and say two thirds equals three quarters. Look at the bars, three quarters is clearly bigger, so that is not the same fraction. Adding does not work, only multiplying does.

visual.caption: Adding 1 to each number changes the amount

steps.say: The other mistake is multiplying only one of the numbers. If you double just the top of two thirds you get four thirds, and that is more than a whole bar. The top and the bottom must always get the same treatment, like sharing fairly. Two times two is four, and three times two is six, so two thirds equals four sixths.
So remember, to make an equivalent fraction, multiply the top and the bottom by the same number, and the fraction keeps its value.

lesson.answer: Multiply the top and the bottom by the same number, and the fraction stays the same size.

practice.question: You buy a granola bar at the store and cut it into four equal pieces, then eat three of them. That is three quarters. Draw a fraction bar split into four parts with three shaded. Now cut each of those four parts into three smaller parts. How many parts are there in the whole bar now, how many are shaded, and what equivalent fraction do you get?
practice.answer: There are twelve parts now and nine are shaded. Three times three is nine on the top, and four times three is twelve on the bottom, so three quarters equals nine twelfths.
